vignette:
At 20, she is one of the youngest people on her audit team, quiet and capable in a way that often makes others assume she is older. She grew up in Oceania in a close family that taught her to be polite, not to make trouble, and to work hard. When she starts her first full-time job as an auditor, she is proud of how quickly she adapts to the routines she once found intimidating: early trains, spreadsheets that stretch for pages, client files arranged in exact order, long days of checking whether numbers match what they should. She likes work that can be verified. It feels safe to have evidence, to be able to trace a discrepancy back to its source.

The stalking begins in a way she almost talks herself out of noticing. A man she sees near the station smiles at her a few times. Then she starts seeing him again outside the office building, then near the café where she buys lunch. At first she explains it away. The city is small, she tells herself. People overlap. When he speaks to her directly for the first time, he already knows her name. He says it casually, as if they have met before. She feels a quick drop in her stomach but forces a smile and keeps walking.

Over the next several weeks, his presence becomes harder to dismiss. He waits outside her office at the end of the day. He appears on her train platform even after she changes her usual schedule. He sends messages from accounts she does not recognize, commenting on what she wore that day, asking why she looked tired, telling her he knows she got home safely. She reads and rereads those messages late at night, trying to understand how much he really knows. She checks her social media and removes old photos, changes passwords, stops posting where she is. She tells herself she is being sensible, but inside she feels something fundamental shift. The ordinary map of her life—work, train, home, shops—no longer feels neutral. Every place seems to contain the possibility of him.

One evening he follows her all the way to her street. She walks faster without wanting to look frightened. She can hear his footsteps adjusting to hers. When she reaches her building, her hands shake so badly she drops her keys. He says softly that she does not need to be scared, that he just wants to talk. She gets inside and locks the door, then stands in the dark of her room listening for sounds in the corridor long after everything is quiet. That night she does not sleep. She sits against the door with her phone in her hand until sunrise.

After that, her life narrows. She changes routes, changes trains, asks colleagues to walk out with her, then feels embarrassed and stops asking. At work she tries to maintain the same level of precision, but her concentration splinters. She loses her place in documents and has to check the same figures three or four times. Small mistakes feel catastrophic. If a client raises their voice on a call, her body reacts before her mind catches up: heart hammering, shoulders tight, breath shallow. When someone passes behind her desk unexpectedly, she jolts so hard she spills coffee over a stack of printed reports. She laughs it off, but afterward she hides in the bathroom and cries in complete silence.

She does not tell many people the full story. Part of her fears they will think she encouraged him somehow by being too friendly, too visible, too careless. Another part cannot bear hearing herself say it out loud. She tells her family only that a man has been “bothering” her. The word feels too small for the reality of how occupied her mind has become. She scans reflections in windows before exiting buildings. She memorizes faces on platforms. She sleeps with the lights on and wakes at the smallest sounds, already flooded with fear. Sometimes she dreams he is standing inside her room, watching her as if he belongs there. She wakes disoriented and checks the locks repeatedly, even when she knows she has already checked them.

Now, months later, the stalking has lessened in frequency but not in impact. Her body still behaves as if contact could happen at any moment. She avoids certain stations entirely and spends money she cannot really spare on rideshares home. She no longer goes out alone after work. Friends invite her to dinner and she invents reasons not to come. Being watched has become a feeling she carries even when she is technically safe. In the office, she keeps her desk immaculate and her monitor angled so no one can approach without her noticing. She remains competent, but the effort is immense. She moves through each day alert, calculating, tired. What unsettles her most is not only what happened, but how thoroughly it has altered her sense of herself. She used to believe that if she was careful and sensible, the world would make sense in return. Now she measures every doorway, every stranger, every trip home against the possibility that she has missed something dangerous again.
